6 Conclusion

We have shown that a small model trained on carefully filtered harbour logs can predict the arrival of a supply boat about as well as the skipper can, which is less impressive than it sounds, because the skipper is often wrong. The interesting result is the failure cases: the model is confident exactly where the logs are thin, in the weeks after a storm, and that is where a human would hedge. We leave the question of how to make it hedge to future work.

Discussion

The packaging format described here has been in use for three years across four archives, and the main lesson is that the manifest matters more than the container. Every archive that tried to infer the structure of a package from its file names eventually gave up and wrote a manifest, and every archive that started with one never had to. The format therefore requires one, and the tools refuse a package that arrives without it, which some depositors have found irritating.

Discussion

The structures predicted for the smaller proteins agree with the measured ones to within the uncertainty of the measurements themselves, which is the strongest claim we can make and the one we have tried hardest to test. For the larger complexes the agreement is weaker, and the disagreements cluster at the interfaces between subunits, where the training data is thinnest and where, not by coincidence, the experimental structures are least certain too. We report both kinds of result side by side.

5. Conclusions

A network that learns the timetable of a ferry from its logs learns the tides first and the school run second, and it forgets the school run the moment the logs stop mentioning it. That is the whole of our result, stated plainly: the regularities that matter to the passengers are the ones the logs record least often, and a model trained on the logs alone will always be surest about the ones that matter least.

General Discussion

People who were told the average of the other judgements moved towards it, and people who were told only the extremes moved away from them, which is the opposite of what the averaging account predicts and roughly what the adding account does. We do not think this settles the matter between the two accounts, but it does suggest that the question was never which rule people follow, only which of the numbers in front of them they believe.

Discussion

The virus isolated from the second cluster differs from the first at eleven positions, all of them outside the region the assay targets, which is why the assay detected both and why we did not notice the difference until the sequences came back. We therefore recommend that laboratories using this assay sequence a sample of their positives as a matter of routine, and we have made our pipeline for doing so available with this preprint.
